summary: Gives recommendations for filtering ICMPv6 messages in firewalls. ICMPv6 is essential for IPv6 to work but has many message types and options, and letting everything through has security risks. The memo suggests what to allow and what to block. It is informational.

eli5.summary: IPv6 needs certain helper messages to work, but some can be abused. This note tells the doorkeeper which to let in and which to turn away.

how to filter icmpv6 in firewalls

subtitle: Which ICMPv6 messages a firewall must let through, which it can leave alone, and which it should block.

tldr.problem: ICMPv6 is essential to IPv6 working, but letting all of it through is a security risk, and the usual IPv4 habit of blocking most ICMP would break IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts ICMPv6 message types into groups (must not drop, should not drop, dropped anyway, policy needed, drop unless justified) for traffic crossing a firewall and for traffic addressed to the firewall itself.
tldr.outcome: Following the lists keeps IPv6 communication working while blocking messages that are mainly security risks.

today: RFC 4890 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the listed metadata. Note that it refers to the neighbor discovery and autoconfiguration specifications as RFC 2461 and RFC 2462.

sections.title: Why ICMPv6 Needs Careful Filtering
sections.content:
ICMPv6 (RFC 4443) is a fundamental part of IPv6. It returns error messages, checks connectivity with echo requests and responses, supports neighbor and router discovery, address autoconfiguration, path MTU determination, multicast listener discovery and mobility. Dropping too much breaks communication. Allowing everything is a major security risk.

Unlike ICMP in IPv4, which was a useful auxiliary protocol that could often be dropped, ICMPv6 cannot be treated that way. Firewall rules therefore need to be more carefully configured than the small blanket rule sets used for ICMP. Some rules depend on whether the firewall protects an individual host, an end site, or a transit site such as an ISP. In general, ISPs should not filter ICMPv6 messages transiting their sites.
sections.eli5: In the old network, the doorkeeper could turn away almost all the helper notes. In the new one, many notes are needed for the house to work, so the doorkeeper has to choose carefully.

sections.title: Classifying ICMPv6 Messages
sections.content:
ICMPv6 has an eight-bit Type field. Types up to and including 127 are error messages, the rest are informational messages. Well-known error messages are generally expected to be allowed to be sent to or through firewalls, while informational messages are mostly subject to policy.

Messages are also classified by reach: end-to-end, local to one link, or any-to-end, which can come from any point on a path back to the source, like Destination Unreachable. End-to-end and any-to-end messages might pass firewalls depending on policy, but local communications must not. Address type and scope matter as well, so filters must look at addresses and not only at message types.
sections.eli5: Some notes are for the whole trip, some are only for neighbors on your own street. Neighbor notes should never leave the street.

sections.title: Threats to Guard Against
sections.content:
Most ICMPv6 messages cannot be authenticated with IPsec, because a site legitimately expects some errors from almost anywhere on the Internet, so firewall filtering is the main defence. The RFC names these concerns.

  • Denial of service: floods of ICMPv6, or error messages that break established sessions.
  • Probing: malformed messages that provoke replies and reveal hosts. The huge IPv6 address space makes this less effective than in IPv4 if addresses are not easily guessed.
  • Redirection attacks: misuse of Redirect for man-in-the-middle or blackholing. Administrators must weigh its efficiency against the risk, for example on open wireless links.
  • Renumbering attacks: spurious Router Renumbering messages. They must be authenticated with IPsec but still should not cross a site boundary.
  • Covert channels: error messages that must pass in both directions could carry hidden conversations or tunneled packets. Deep packet inspection of the embedded packet can help.
sections.eli5: Bad guys can use these helper notes to flood a house, snoop around, send people the wrong way, or sneak secret messages out. The doorkeeper has to stop those without blocking the useful notes.

sections.title: Rules for Traffic Crossing the Firewall
sections.content:
For transit traffic the RFC groups message types. Many link-local messages need no rule, because routers do not forward them and receivers check that the hop limit is still 255 or that the source is link-local. A firewall that is a bridge must instead let them through.

  • Must not be dropped: Destination Unreachable (Type 1, all codes), Packet Too Big (Type 2), Time Exceeded (Type 3, code 0), Parameter Problem (Type 4, codes 1 and 2), and Echo Request and Response (Types 128 and 129). Echo must pass for Teredo tunneling to nodes on the site.
  • Normally should not be dropped: Time Exceeded code 1, Parameter Problem code 0, and the Mobile IPv6 messages (Types 144 to 147).
  • Dropped anyway: neighbor and router discovery, MLD, SEND certificate path and multicast router discovery messages, which stay on the link.
  • Policy needed: the experimental Seamoby message (Type 150) and unallocated error and informational types.
  • Drop unless a good case is made: Node Information Query and Response (Types 139 and 140), Router Renumbering (Type 138), experimental types 100, 101, 200 and 201, and extension types 127 and 255.
sections.eli5: Error notes and the are-you-there ping must always get through. Notes meant only for the same street are already stopped at the corner. A few odd notes should be kept out unless there is a good reason.

sections.title: Rules for Traffic to the Firewall Itself
sections.content:
Messages addressed to an interface on the firewall follow a similar scheme. The same error and echo messages must not be dropped, and so must the messages that configure the node and maintain unicast and multicast communication: Router and Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, Inverse Neighbor Discovery, multicast listener messages, SEND certificate path messages and multicast router discovery messages.

Redirect (Type 137) and Node Information messages need an explicit decision, and the RFC notes that conformant nodes provide configuration controls for Redirect so specific filter rules are only needed in special cases, such as accepting Redirect on private but not public interfaces. Router Renumbering must be authenticated with IPsec, so filtering it is not essential. Mobile IPv6 messages may be dropped, especially on public interfaces, if the firewall is not also a home agent. The RFC also gives an example Linux Netfilter script in Appendix B.
sections.eli5: The doorkeeper is also a person who has to talk to others. So the doorkeeper must accept the notes needed to stay connected to the neighbors, but can choose whether to follow route tips.
